Dear Esther is very interesting. It was initially released as a free game using Valve's Source engine (I believe). It met with a very positive response and the developer (The Chinese Room) then went ahead and rebuilt it with a more modern engine (which is shown in this video). I have both versions and as far as I can tell, other than the graphics, they are basically identical. The developer subsequently produced the Amnesia series (Amnesia: Dark Descent, and Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs).

It should be noted that Dear Esther is NOT a game in any sense although it contains some puzzle-like elements. It is a landscape you walk and explore. There are writings and other things that you come across which suggest some type of backstory, but there is no real goal. It is a fairly unique experience and more akin to a dreamworld. I believe it is being ported to a console. I picked it up on a Steam sale for dirt-cheap a couple of years ago. It is worth buying the paid version if it is cheap as the graphics really enhance the experience over the free version. If, however, it isn't less than $5, grab the free version if you're curious.

I wouldn't necessarily refer to Dear Esther as a "walking sim" insofar as that sounds a bit pejorative. Dear Esther was initially a free mod, so nobody buying the (graphically enhanced) commercial version should have expected it to be anything different (The Chinese Room never represented it as otherwise). It clearly never was a "game" nor a sim...nor was it designed to be. It is a fairly unique experiential presentation that falls outside the bounds of normal gaming. To put it more bluntly for those who haven't "played" it, Dear Esther is more of an experimental form of immersive storytelling--but without a clear, coherent narrative. That's how it is designed and presented. It is really difficult to classify because it is so unique. I'd call it "literary" in nature, solely because it forces the audience to think about what is presented and encourages them to form a subjective opinion on the backstory. It is replete with both allusion and the fantastic, but takes place in what otherwise might be described as "the real world."

It is a difficult to describe Dear Esther to folks who haven't "played" it because each person will bring their own expectations. I'd wager that folks who are expecting a "game" experience will be sorely let down as will folks who don't appreciate or understand what the developers were going for. It is, however, beautifully rendered and executed nearly flawlessly. I believe it fulfilled the developers artistic vision quite well. Whether or not it resonates with a broader audience as a standalone piece of art is subjective. I enjoyed it thoroughly. I think in another 10-20 years, folks will still look back on Dear Esther as a proto-VR piece that inspired a new genre of experiential storytelling.

From the Steam description (emphasis is mine):

Two years in the making, the highly anticipated Indie remake of the cult mod Dear Esther arrives on PC. Dear Esther immerses you in a stunningly realised world, a remote and desolate island somewhere in the outer Hebrides. As you step forwards, a voice begins to read fragments of a letter: "Dear Esther..." - and so begins a journey through one of the most original first-person games of recent years. Abandoning traditional gameplay for a pure story-driven experience, Dear Esther fuses its beautiful environments with a breathtaking soundtrack to tell a powerful story of love, loss, guilt and redemption.

Forget the normal rules of play; if nothing seems real here, it’s because it may just be all a delusion. What is the significance of the aerial -- What happened on the motorway -- is the island real or imagined -- who is Esther and why has she chosen to summon you here? From Dear Esther's website (FAQ):

A. Dear Esther is a poetic ghost story told using game technologies. Of course you DO have a point--it's built using a game engine and sold on Steam (and probably other gaming stores). Anyone who just runs across it isn't likely to read for the full description or seek out the FAQ on the developer's website. Most folks purchasing it on Steam will likely expect a traditional game with some type of puzzles or linear narrative. I'm just pointing out that the developer never intended it to be that and never hid the fact that it wasn't. And the fact that anyone could download the full, free version of it to get a taste sort of gives them a free pass on any criticism that they failed to deliver on expectations.

Since you and I have both completed Dear Esther, I'm assuming our divergent opinions on it are mostly rooted in expectations and personal taste...which I have no problem with. For those who haven't gone through it, I'd recommend reading the FAQ on the Dear Esther site as they do a decent job explaining what they were going for (TLDR a William S. Burroughs/Phillip K. Dick type of surreal experience). I strongly believe that you can't judge it against any games. It's sort of like comparing The Avenger's films to Alejandro Jodorowsky "El Topo"--yeah, both are stories rendered on film, but "El Topo" doesn't purport to be a "Hollywood" film, nor does it adhere to traditional narrative structure or presentation--it's a unique piece of art that merely shares the same medium as The Avengers...but in substance it has to be judged by different standards and will succeed or fail in large part based on what expectations you bring to it. If you're the type of person who watches a film like El Topo and gets upset that it's not a traditional Western, then you might be the type of person who runs through Dear Esther and gets annoyed it's not more like Myst. I recently played through Pneuma: Breath of Life and was struck how it seemed influenced by Dear Esther (although it is clearly a puzzle-game). But honestly, I think Dear Esther is most likely to inspire a new type of non-gaming way of open-ended storytelling that will probably flourish in VR.

Story, graphics, audio are all just supplements for an overall greater product.
